title: The Day the Wind Stopped
hook: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, Indra strikes him down, and the wind god stops: every creature chokes
carry: pranayama tends breath as a sacred gift
tomorrow: speech, mind or breath: who really holds the body up?

segments.voice: Last week closed on Hindu worship caring for God, dawn to night: a temple's bedtime and its dawn song, and Rama woken with words.

A baby wakes up hungry. Above him, the rising sun glows red, and he thinks it's a fruit. So he jumps for it. This is Hanuman, son of Vayu, the wind, and in the Ramayana's telling he leaps right up into the sky. Indra, king of the gods, alarmed, strikes him with his thunderbolt, and the child falls onto a mountain, his jaw broken. Then his father does something terrible and quiet. Vayu stops. Today, the day the wind stopped blowing, and what it teaches about breath.
screen: `A BABY JUMPS FOR THE SUN.` → `THE THUNDERBOLT.` → `THE WIND STOPS.`

segments.voice: Vayu, grieving, takes his son into a cave and holds still. And because the wind is also the breath in every body, everything chokes. Creatures can't breathe, the text says; their bodies go stiff like wood; the gods themselves are in distress. They run to Brahma, the creator, who comes to the cave and revives the child, and the wind moves again. Then the gods, one by one, give Hanuman boons, and the Ramayana ties his name to that broken jaw, hanu. Here is the teaching, named plainly. In Hindu thought, breath isn't just air. Vayu is a god, and prana, breath, is life itself, given to every body. That's why yoga treats breath with care. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras make breath practice, pranayama, one of yoga's eight limbs, and describe it simply: the breath out, the breath in and the pause, watched by place, by time and by number, becomes long and fine. That's a description, not a promise. It doesn't say a pattern heals illness, and it gives no count of seconds. So this week, every claim about breath gets one of three labels: the text says, tradition says, or a doctor decides. One plain safety line, because breath work isn't neutral. Anyone with a heart or lung condition, anyone pregnant, anyone who gets dizzy or anxious with breath exercises keeps to easy natural breathing and asks a doctor before any holding of the breath. Today's practice holds nothing. It only watches, the way you'd look after a gift.
screen: `THE WIND STOPS; EVERYTHING CHOKES` · `VAYU: BREATH AS A GOD` · `PRANAYAMA: ONE OF EIGHT LIMBS` · `TEXT, TRADITION, OR A DOCTOR`

segments.voice: Let the breath do whatever it's doing, and watch it by place, where it's felt most, then by time, whether the in-breath runs longer than the out-breath, then by number, counting a few breaths from one to five, without changing anything. If it grows longer and finer on its own, notice that; if it doesn't, that's an honest result too. If you pray, let each out-breath be a small thanks to the One who gives it.
The breath again. When Vayu stood still, every creature choked; in the Yoga Sutras, breath watched by place, time and number becomes long and fine. Today's word.
Your line: pranayama tends breath as a sacred gift. The text says, tradition says, a doctor decides. That's today, done.

fork.setup: you're Vayu. your baby son has been struck down by Indra's thunderbolt. what does the wind do?
options: stop moving, and take the child into a cave.
keep blowing as if nothing happened.
fork.reveal: Vayu holds still, and every creature chokes. the gods run to Brahma, the child lives, and the wind moves again: breath is the life of everything.

original.note: Sanskrit vayu: wind, and the wind god, Hanuman's father. the same word names the breaths that move in the body.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 35–36 (the infant Hanuman leaps at the sun; Indra's thunderbolt breaks his jaw; Vayu withdraws into a cave and beings cannot breathe; the gods go to Brahma, who revives the child; the gods' boons; the name from hanu)
Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 66 (Jambavan retells Hanuman's birth and leap at the sun)
Yoga Sutras 2.29 (the eight limbs, pranayama among them)
Yoga Sutras 2.49 (pranayama follows posture: a pause in the flow of in-breath and out-breath)
Yoga Sutras 2.50 (the outward, inward and held movement, observed by place, time and number, becomes long and subtle)
